newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: RTRS-Protests turn violent in Papua New Guinea.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Protests turn violent in Papua New Guinea.

text.p: The government of Papua New Guinea faced a fresh challenge to its authority on Wednesday as army officers rallied behind their sacked commander and a street protest erupted in violence.

Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan, criticised internationally for a plan to use foreign mercenaries against local rebels, dismissed the commander on Monday after he demanded that Chan and other ministers resign.

Defence force commander Jerry Singirok said on Tuesday he accepted his dismissal but remained holed up on Wednesday in Port Moresby's main barracks, where at least 1,500 protesters arrived to back him in his campaign against Chan.

The protesters planned to march on parliament house and tried to entice soldiers to join them. The soldiers remained in barracks but cheered their support as a senior officer told the crowd that 40 foreign mercenaries must leave the country.
Violence followed within hours when demonstrators broke loose from the crowd and started looting nearby shops.
In a first wave, about 200 demonstrators broke loose and attacked two supermarkets. Police fired tear gas into the crowd and live ammunition over their heads to calm the situation.
Protest leaders then handed over a petition demanding the resignation of Chan and two other senior ministers within 24 hours and the demonstration officially dispersed.

But the bulk of the protesters, many of them laughing, ran up a main city street to loot another supermarket. Heavily-armed police fired teargas at the looters and more live rounds over their heads before a tense standoff developed.
Soldiers, confined to barracks since the South Pacific nation's crisis began on Monday, did not get involved.
Wednesday's scenes, on what a senior police officer said was a "make-or-break day", showed that one of the worst crises in the South Pacific nation's short history was far from over.
Papua New Guinea, which has a mainly-Melanesian population of 4.3 million, won independence from Australia in 1975 and remains a member of the old British Commonwealth.

Before the violence, an army major told protesters outside the barracks that the army was opposed to the mercenary plan and foreign soldiers detained by the army since Monday would soon leave the country.

The mercenaries arrived in February to train PNG soldiers and help end the costly nine-year conflict on Bougainville, a resource-rich island northeast of Port Moresby. The first group was expected to leave Papua New Guinea later on Wednesday.
And the officer, Major Walter Enuma, said the defence force still considered Singirok to be its commander -- even though he had been officially sacked by Chan.

"The mercenaries have come in here and undermined the constitutional rule of this country," Enuma, a handgun in one hand and loud-hailer in the other, told cheering protesters outside the city's Murray barracks.
"I think they have undermined the dedication and loyalty of the soldiers and police," Enuma said.

Enuma told reporters that senior army officers were to meet to decide whether the army would join a civil protest march against Chan, who on Monday sacked Singirok after the rebellious general gave Chan a 48-hour deadline to quit.
A government official said troops remained loyal to the government and acting commander Colonel Alfred Aikung.
"They're only a small percentage of those in the defence force but obviously they can cause trouble as they hold the guns," the official said.
Australia has led international condemnation of Chan's plan to use mercenaries on Bougainville, although it backed the prime minister in his decision to sack Singirok.

Prime Minister John Howard told parliament on Wednesday that he was sending a personal emissary to help resolve the crisis. Officials said Philip Flood, Australia's top diplomat, would fly to Port Moresby on Wednesday night.
